words.definition: to succeed in reaching a goal, usually through hard work

meet.sentence: After two years of training, Noa finally {achieved} her goal of running a marathon.

questions.prompt: to succeed in reaching a goal, usually through hard work

questions.sentence: With better planning, the team could {_} much better results next year.
Our team worked hard and {achieved} first place in the competition.
questions.explain: Correct. You achieve a goal, a result or a place in a competition.

questions.sentence: He {achieved} the bus by running all the way to the station.
questions.explain: You catch a bus. Achieve is for goals and results you work for.

questions.them: You got 100 in the math Bagrut?! How?? 😱
questions.me: Lots of practice! If you work hard, you can {_} anything.

questions.them: Did the class reach its goal for the charity run?
questions.me: Yes! We raised 5,000 shekels. We {_} our goal two weeks early.

questions.sentence: Getting into the national team was a huge {_} for the whole school.
questions.hint: You need a noun here. Many nouns made from verbs end in -ment.

options.text: She {achieved} her dream of becoming a doctor.
The company {achieved} record sales this year.
I {achieved} my keys under the sofa.
They {achieved} a cold after the trip.

questions.explain: You achieve goals, dreams and results. You find keys and catch a cold.

questions.sentence: Setting small, {_} goals helps students stay motivated.
questions.explain: Before 'goals' you need an adjective: achievable = possible to reach.

words.definition: to keep something going over a long period of time

meet.sentence: Our town cannot {sustain} its water supply if people keep wasting so much.

questions.prompt: to keep something going over a long period of time

questions.sentence: Without enough food and water, the island could not {_} life for long.
She {sustained} the door quickly so the cat couldn't get out.
questions.explain: Sustain means to keep something going over time. For a door, you would shut or close it.

questions.them: Our school started a recycling program, but I bet it stops in a month 🙄
questions.me: Not if we all help. We can {_} it for years!

questions.them: You've been running every morning for a year?! How do you keep it up?
questions.me: Small steps. That's the only way to {_} a habit for so long.

questions.sentence: We need more {_} ways to produce energy, like solar and wind power.
questions.hint: You need an adjective before 'ways'. Many adjectives end in -able.

questions.sentence: The economy grew quickly, but the growth was not {sustained} for long.
questions.explain: Correct. Sustained growth is growth that continues over time.

questions.sentence: The city is famous for its focus on {_}, with bike lanes and green roofs everywhere.
questions.explain: After 'its focus on' you need a noun: sustainability.

words.definition: to show or make known something that was hidden or secret

meet.sentence: The study {revealed} that most teenagers sleep less than they need.

questions.prompt: to show or make known something that was hidden or secret

questions.sentence: The police hope the cameras will {_} who broke into the shop.
The new report {revealed} that air pollution in the city had doubled.
questions.explain: Correct. A report or study can reveal (show) information that wasn't known.

questions.sentence: Please {reveal} the window, it's really hot in here.
questions.explain: Reveal is for secrets and information. For a window, you open it.

questions.them: Did you see the magic show?? How did he do the coin trick?!
questions.me: No idea! He refused to {_} his secret 🤐

questions.them: So... is the surprise party still a secret? 🎉
questions.me: Yes! Don't {_} anything to Yael until Friday!

questions.sentence: The interview was very {_}: we learned a lot about her private life.
questions.hint: You need an adjective that describes the interview. Try the -ing form.

questions.sentence: Her sudden {_} that she was leaving the band shocked her fans.
questions.explain: After 'her sudden' you need a noun: revelation.

words.definition: to refuse to accept or agree to something

meet.sentence: The principal {rejected} our idea to start school at ten o'clock.

questions.prompt: to refuse to accept or agree to something

questions.sentence: The committee voted to {_} the plan because it was far too expensive.
The university {rejected} his application, so he applied again the next year.
questions.explain: Correct. You can reject an application, an offer or an idea.

questions.sentence: I {rejected} my homework in my bag so I wouldn't lose it.
questions.explain: Reject means to refuse something. You put homework in your bag.

questions.them: Did you ask your parents about the trip to Eilat?
questions.me: Yes 😩 They {_} the idea. They said it's too far.

questions.them: The team offered you the captain role? That's amazing!
questions.me: I know, but I'm going to {_} it. I don't have time this year.

questions.sentence: Getting a {_} letter from a college can be very painful.
questions.hint: You need a noun before 'letter'. Many nouns end in -ion.

options.text: {Rejected} by three publishers, the book later became a bestseller.
She felt {rejected} when nobody invited her to the party.
The body can {reject} a new organ after a transplant.
He {rejected} the ball straight into the net.

questions.explain: Reject can also describe feelings (to feel rejected) and the body refusing a transplant. You kick a ball into the net.

words.definition: to give money, time or ideas to help something, together with other people

meet.sentence: Every student {contributed} 20 shekels to buy a present for the teacher.
options: gave as part of a group

questions.prompt: to give money, time or ideas to help something, together with other people

questions.sentence: Everyone in the group should {_} at least one idea to the project.
Lack of sleep can {contribute} to poor grades.
questions.explain: Correct. Contribute to can also mean 'be one of the causes of' something.

questions.sentence: I {contributed} a new phone from the store yesterday.
questions.explain: Contribute means to give to a shared goal. From a store, you buy something.

questions.them: We're collecting money for the animal shelter. Want to help? 🐶
questions.me: Of course! I'd love to {_}. How much do you need?

questions.them: Why are you staying late after school every day?
questions.me: I volunteer at the library. I want to {_} something to my community.

questions.sentence: Thank you for your generous {_} to our school fair.
questions.hint: You need a noun after 'your generous'. Many nouns end in -ion.

questions.sentence: Doctors say that too much screen time may {_} to anxiety in teenagers.
questions.explain: Contribute to can mean 'help cause'. Here, screen time is one of the causes of anxiety.

words.definition: an advantage or good result that you get from something

meet.sentence: One big {benefit} of living near the sea is the fresh air.

questions.prompt: an advantage or good result that you get from something

questions.sentence: Regular exercise has many health {_}, like better sleep and a stronger heart.
Learning a second language has many {benefits}, like better job opportunities.
questions.explain: Correct. A benefit is a good result or advantage.

questions.sentence: I hurt my knee, and the {benefit} lasted for weeks.
questions.explain: A benefit is something good. For a knee, you'd talk about the pain or the injury.

questions.them: Why do you wake up at 6 to study? That's crazy 😴
questions.me: The {_} is that my brain is fresh and the house is quiet.

questions.them: Is the new school app actually useful?
questions.me: Yes! The main {_} is that you can see all your grades in one place.

questions.sentence: Drinking enough water is {_} for your concentration.
questions.hint: You need an adjective after 'is'. This one ends in -ial.

questions.sentence: Everyone will {_} from the new library, from small kids to grandparents.
questions.explain: Benefit can also be a verb: to benefit from something = to get something good from it.

words.definition: something that stops people or things from moving forward or doing something

meet.sentence: For many new immigrants, language is the biggest {barrier} to finding a job.

questions.prompt: something that stops people or things from moving forward or doing something

questions.sentence: The police put up a {_} to stop cars from entering the street during the marathon.
Not knowing the local language can be a {barrier} when you move abroad.
questions.explain: Correct. A barrier can be physical (a fence) or not (a language barrier).

questions.sentence: Winning the prize was a great {barrier} for the whole team.
questions.explain: A barrier blocks you. Winning a prize is an achievement.

questions.them: How was your trip to Japan? Did you understand anyone? 😅
questions.me: Not really. The language {_} was hard, but people were super kind.

questions.them: Why didn't more students sign up for the trip?
questions.me: The price was the main {_}. It's way too expensive for most families.

options.text: Cost is a major {barrier} to higher education.
Breaking the sound {barrier} was a historic moment.
The wall was built as a {barrier} against floods.
She gave me a {barrier} for my birthday.

questions.explain: A barrier can block movement (a flood barrier), progress (cost) or mark a limit (the sound barrier). It isn't a present.

words.definition: to deal with a problem; also, to speak to a person or a group

meet.sentence: The new government promised to {address} the housing crisis quickly.

questions.prompt: to start dealing with a problem
to speak to a group of people formally

questions.sentence: The school must {_} the problem of bullying before it gets worse.
The principal will {_} all the students at the end-of-year ceremony.
The report {addresses} the main causes of air pollution.
questions.explain: Correct. To address an issue is to deal with it or discuss it.

questions.sentence: I {addressed} a delicious cake for my mom's birthday.
questions.explain: Address means to deal with a problem or speak to people. You bake a cake.

questions.them: The Wi-Fi at school is SO slow. Is anyone doing anything about it?
questions.me: The principal said they'll {_} the problem next week.

questions.them: Why are you so nervous today?
questions.me: I have to {_} the whole school at the assembly tomorrow 😬

questions.sentence: The president {addressed} the nation on TV last night.
questions.explain: Correct. To address a group is to give a formal speech to it.

questions.sentence: Please {_} all questions to the school secretary, not to the teachers.
questions.explain: Address can also mean to send or direct questions or a letter to someone.

words.definition: to organize and do something, like research or a survey; also, to lead an orchestra

meet.sentence: Our class {conducted} a survey about students' sleeping habits.

questions.prompt: to organize and do an activity, such as research or an experiment
to stand in front of musicians and direct them

questions.sentence: Scientists {_} experiments to test whether the new medicine is safe.
My uncle will {_} the orchestra at tonight's concert.
The police are {conducting} an investigation into the robbery.
questions.explain: Correct. You conduct an investigation, a survey or research.

questions.sentence: She {conducted} a glass of water because she was thirsty.
questions.explain: Conduct means to carry out an activity or lead musicians. You drink water.

questions.them: What's your science project about?
questions.me: We're going to {_} an experiment with plants and music 🌱🎵

questions.them: Who's the man waving the stick in front of the orchestra?
questions.me: That's Mr. Levi! He'll {_} the school orchestra tonight.

questions.sentence: The {_} raised his hands, and the orchestra began to play.
questions.hint: You need a noun for a person. Many words for people end in -or or -er.

questions.sentence: Metals like copper {_} electricity very well.
questions.explain: Conduct also means to let heat or electricity pass through.

words.definition: to keep something in good condition or at the same level; also, to keep saying that something is true

meet.sentence: It's hard to {maintain} good grades when you work every evening.

questions.prompt: to keep something at the same level or in good condition
to keep saying that something is true, even when others disagree

questions.sentence: Old buildings cost a lot of money to {_}.
He continues to {_} that he is innocent, but the police don't believe him.
Athletes need to {maintain} a healthy diet all year round.
questions.explain: Correct. You maintain a diet, a level, a speed or a building.

questions.sentence: I {maintained} my friend a funny video last night.
questions.explain: Maintain means to keep something going or in good condition. You send someone a video.

questions.them: Your bike looks brand new! Didn't you buy it like 5 years ago?
questions.me: Yes! I clean it every week. You have to {_} a bike if you want it to last.

questions.them: Did Ben admit he ate your sandwich? 🥪
questions.me: No way. He still {_} that it was the dog!

questions.sentence: The pool is closed today for {_}. It will open again tomorrow.
questions.hint: You need a noun. Careful with the spelling: maintain → mainten…

questions.sentence: Scientists {maintain} that the climate is changing faster than expected.
questions.explain: Correct. Maintain can mean to say firmly that something is true.

questions.sentence: The two countries have {_} good relations for over fifty years.
questions.explain: 'For over fifty years' tells you it's about keeping something going: maintained.

words.definition: to change your behaviour, or change something, so it fits a new situation

meet.sentence: It took my family a few months to {adapt} to life in a new country.
options: get used to it by changing

questions.prompt: to change your behaviour, or change something, so it fits a new situation

questions.sentence: Animals in the desert {_} to the heat by sleeping during the day.
The movie was {adapted} from a famous novel.
questions.explain: Correct. A book can be adapted (changed) into a movie.

questions.sentence: My aunt {adapted} a baby girl from Ethiopia.
questions.explain: Careful: you adopt a child (take them into your family). Adapt means to change to fit a new situation.

questions.them: How's the new school? Do you miss your old friends?
questions.me: A little, but I'm starting to {_}. People here are nice 🙂

questions.them: Wait, you changed the whole recipe? Why?
questions.me: My sister is vegan, so I had to {_} it a bit 🥦

questions.sentence: Moving to a new city every year is easier for children who are {_}.
questions.hint: You need an adjective after 'are'. Many adjectives end in -able.

questions.sentence: The book was {_} into a TV series with eight episodes.
questions.explain: Adapt = change something to fit a new form. Adopt = take as your own (a child, an idea).

words.definition: to produce a change in someone or something

meet.sentence: Lack of sleep can {affect} your mood and your memory.

questions.prompt: to produce a change in someone or something

questions.sentence: The heavy rain will {_} traffic all over the city tomorrow.
Social media can {affect} how teenagers see themselves.
questions.explain: Correct. Affect is a verb: to influence or change something.

questions.sentence: The medicine had a strong {affect} on her headache.
questions.explain: Careful: here you need the noun, effect. Affect is the verb; effect is the noun.

questions.them: Why are you so tired today? 🥱
questions.me: I stayed up until 3. It always {_} my concentration the next day.

questions.them: Is it true that the new road will close the park?
questions.me: Yes, and it will {_} everyone who lives nearby.

options.text: The {effect} of the war was huge.
The new rule will {effect} all students.

questions.explain: Affect is the verb (to influence). Effect is the noun (the result).

questions.sentence: Hundreds of families were {_} by the floods.
questions.explain: Affected = influenced or harmed by something.
